title: Renunciation and action arrive at the same place

verses.sa: अर्जुन उवाचसंन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि । यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्िचतम् ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna says: Krishna, you praise both renunciation of action and yoga of action. Tell me clearly which one is definitely better for my welfare.
verses.angle: Arjuna asks which of the two paths is better
verses.speaker: Arjuna

intro.text: Krishna has spoken at length about acting and renouncing, and Arjuna now asks him to stop praising both. He wants to know which single path is truly better.

body.text: Arjuna says: Krishna, you praise both renunciation of action and yoga of action. Tell me clearly which one is definitely better for my welfare. Arjuna points out that Krishna praises both renunciation and action, and asks him to choose one path that is clearly better for his welfare. Krishna replies that both paths lead to the highest good, but acting with discipline is better than renouncing action.

verses.sa: श्री भगवानुवाचसंन्यासः कर्मयोगश्च निःश्रेयसकरावुभौ । तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते ॥
verses.tr: Renunciation and karma yoga both lead to the highest good, but karma yoga is better than renouncing action.
verses.angle: Visishyate: the word that ranks the two paths
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for the word that makes one path outrank the other, right after Krishna says both paths lead to the highest good.

body.text: Renunciation and karma yoga both lead to the highest good, but karma yoga is better than renouncing action. The word is visishyate, which means is superior. Krishna first says both paths bring the highest good, and then he adds that karma yoga is superior to renunciation of action. Krishna then describes the person who is truly free from desire and hate, and is always a true renunciant.

verses.sa: ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति । निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते ॥
verses.tr: One who neither hates nor desires is always a renunciant. Free from opposites, such a person is easily released from bondage, O mighty-armed one.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now sharpens the teaching. Real renunciation means inner freedom from hatred, craving, and the tug of opposites, whatever one's outward life.

body.text: One who neither hates nor desires is always a renunciant. Free from opposites, such a person is easily released from bondage, O mighty-armed one. Listen to nir-dvandva, free from opposites, and what that word reveals here. A true renunciant is not someone who abandons action, but someone who drops hatred and craving. Freedom comes when inner opposites no longer pull the mind. Krishna now shows that the wise see no conflict between renunciation and yoga, because both paths lead to the same fruit.

verses.sa: सांख्ययोगौ पृथग्बालाः प्रवदन्ति न पण्डिताः । एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम् ॥
verses.tr: The unwise say that renunciation and yoga lead to different results. The wise see that one who is firmly established in either reaches the same fruit.
verses.angle: balah, the unwise, dismiss two paths
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now calls the idea that two paths lead to different places a childish mistake. Listen to who he calls childish and why.

body.text: The unwise say that renunciation and yoga lead to different results. The wise see that one who is firmly established in either reaches the same fruit. The word balah means the unwise or childish. It is not a polite disagreement, but a dismissal of those who see renunciation and yoga as separate roads. The wise see that one established in either path reaches the same fruit, and the next verse shows what that fruit is.

verses.sa: यत्सांख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते । एकं सांख्यं च योगं च यः पश्यति स पश्यति ॥
verses.tr: The state reached by the wise is also reached through yoga. One who sees wisdom and yoga as one sees rightly.
verses.angle: Wisdom and action as one path
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Arjuna is still stuck on whether to fight or to renounce. What does Krishna say to untangle this? Listen to how he joins the two paths.

body.text: The state reached by the wise is also reached through yoga. One who sees wisdom and yoga as one sees rightly. Krishna says the state reached by wisdom is also reached through action. The one who sees both as a single path sees clearly, and that clarity is the true sight. Krishna then says that renunciation without action is hard, and the disciplined path of yoga leads to the supreme reality.

verses.sa: संन्यासस्तु महाबाहो दुःखमाप्तुमयोगतः । योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म नचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥
verses.tr: But, mighty-armed one, renunciation without yoga is hard to attain. The disciplined seeker in yoga quickly reaches the supreme reality.
verses.speaker: Krishna

body.text: But, mighty-armed one, renunciation without yoga is hard to attain. The disciplined seeker in yoga quickly reaches the supreme reality. Mighty-armed Arjuna hears that renunciation without yoga is hard, while a disciplined yogi reaches Brahman quickly. The disciplined yogi sees the same self in all beings and acts without being tainted by action.

verses.sa: योगयुक्तो विशुद्धात्मा विजितात्मा जितेन्द्रियः । सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मा कुर्वन्नपि न लिप्यते ॥
verses.tr: A disciplined yogi, pure in mind, self-mastered, and senses conquered, sees the same self in all beings and is not tainted by action while acting.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to listen for one Sanskrit word that shows exactly where the stain on action comes from.

body.text: A disciplined yogi, pure in mind, self-mastered, and senses conquered, sees the same self in all beings and is not tainted by action while acting. The word is visuddhatma, pure inner being. A person acts without being stained not because the work is light, but because the inner being itself has been made pure, so no action can stick to it. Krishna then shows that even while doing all this, the knower of reality should think, 'I do nothing at all.'

verses.sa: नैव किंचित्करोमीति युक्तो मन्येत तत्त्ववित् । पश्यन् श्रृणवन्स्पृशञ्जिघ्रन्नश्नन्गच्छन्स्वपन् श्वसन् ॥
verses.tr: The knower of reality should think, "I do nothing at all," while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, taking, speaking, discarding, sleeping, breathing, and opening and closing the eyes.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Arjuna is frozen between action and collapse. Krishna now describes the inner vision of the wise person who still moves through the world.

body.text: The knower of reality should think, "I do nothing at all," while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, taking, speaking, discarding, sleeping, breathing, and opening and closing the eyes. The knower of reality thinks, 'I do nothing at all,' while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, and breathing. The body is active, but the knower claims no doership for it. Krishna adds that the senses move among their objects, even while the wise person is speaking, eating, or sleeping.

verses.tr: Even while speaking, releasing, taking, opening, and closing the eyes, the wise know: the senses move among their objects.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna carries on from the idea of non-action, showing how the body and senses keep moving.

body.text: Even while speaking, releasing, taking, opening, and closing the eyes, the wise know: the senses move among their objects. Notice the exact phrase 'the senses move among sense-objects.' Krishna says that speaking, taking, and blinking are not the self acting, but the senses simply moving among their objects. Krishna now turns to the one who offers every action to Brahman and remains untainted by sin.

verses.sa: ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः । लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥
verses.tr: One who offers actions to Brahman, renounces attachment, and acts is not stained by wrongdoing, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
verses.angle: Tyaktva: abandoning attachment to act without stain
verses.speaker: Krishna

body.text: One who offers actions to Brahman, renounces attachment, and acts is not stained by wrongdoing, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water. The word tyaktva, having abandoned, is the key. It is not the act that binds, but the attachment to the result. By leaving that behind, a person acts in the world like a lotus leaf in water, and remains unstained. Krishna then explains that this inner purification is the true purpose of performing action with the body and mind.

verses.sa: कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि । योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वाऽऽत्मशुद्धये ॥
verses.tr: Yogis perform action with body, mind, intellect, and the senses, giving up attachment, only for inner purification.
verses.angle: tyaktva: the act of giving up attachment
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Picture a practitioner who keeps working but stays untouched by the outcome. This verse lists every part of a person that acts, and the one thing that is left behind.

body.text: Yogis perform action with body, mind, intellect, and the senses, giving up attachment, only for inner purification. The word tyaktva means having given up, and it is the turning point of the verse. The yogi performs action with body, mind, intellect, and senses, yet the one thing dropped is attachment. Krishna then explains what happens when this letting go is done, and what happens when it is not.

verses.sa: युक्तः कर्मफलं त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम् । अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते ॥
verses.tr: The disciplined one gives up the fruit of action and attains steady peace. The undisciplined one, clinging to results through desire, becomes bound.
verses.angle: Tyaktva: the single act of letting go
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for the word tyaktva, having given up. Notice how Krishna places it right before the peace that follows.

body.text: The disciplined one gives up the fruit of action and attains steady peace. The undisciplined one, clinging to results through desire, becomes bound. The word tyaktva, having given up, stands between the fruit of action and steady peace. This single word marks the shift from craving to release. Krishna now turns to the one who has not given up, showing how desire becomes the chain that binds.

verses.sa: सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी । नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन्न कारयन् ॥
verses.tr: The embodied one, who has mastered the senses and mind, dwells happily in the city of nine gates, mentally renouncing all actions, neither doing nor causing action.
verses.angle: The body as a nine-gated city
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has been teaching Arjuna about action without attachment, and now he points to a deeper state. Listen to how he describes the self-mastered person's inner stillness.

body.text: The embodied one, who has mastered the senses and mind, dwells happily in the city of nine gates, mentally renouncing all actions, neither doing nor causing action. Krishna calls the body a city with nine gates. Inside that city, the self-mastered one dwells happily by letting go of all actions in the mind, never acting and never causing others to act. Krishna then explains that nature alone performs all actions, leaving the self free from doership.

verses.sa: न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः । न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते ॥
verses.tr: The supreme being creates neither doership nor actions nor the link between action and result for people. Nature alone keeps moving.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna carries on from the idea of mental renunciation by explaining what the supreme being actually creates.

body.text: The supreme being creates neither doership nor actions nor the link between action and result for people. Nature alone keeps moving. The key actor here is svabhava, nature. While the Lord creates no doer, no action, and no binding result, nature alone keeps moving forward on its own. Krishna then explains that the all-pervading Lord takes neither wrongdoing nor good deeds, and that knowledge is covered by ignorance.
